source.version_note: Frontiers in Ophthalmology 6, article 1766974, published 3 March 2026; received 13 December 2025, revised 5 February and accepted 15 February 2026. No future-date discrepancy against the review date.
source.verification_method: All seven supplied pages and all 21 references read. All three tables visually inspected, including the counts and percentages on pages 3–5. Main and corrected reference identities checked against Crossref and public publisher metadata. Selected contingency-table tests independently reconstructed from printed counts; raw data, exact questionnaire and supplementary document not independently read.

citation.title: Artificial intelligence in ophthalmology: trust, bias, and responsibility from the perspective of medical students and ophthalmologists

reading.source_scope_note: Exploratory convenience survey of hypothetical preferences, not observed clinical conduct or measured AI safety. Substantial cross-table disagreements remain unresolved; do not pool or repair the printed data by guessing. Mechanism interpretations are expressly acknowledged as speculative by the authors.
access_limits: No respondent-level dataset, scoring code, full item wording/order or prespecified analysis retrieved. The data-availability statement offers data on request; no author contact was made.

The public article identifies Supplementary File 1, Summary of survey-assessed parameters and demographics, and its file metadata identifies a .doc document. Its contents were not retrieved/read in this review; do not claim that a full questionnaire is absent from every source.
Bibliographic checks of reference 3 and the psychiatry survey are identity checks, not independent full-paper reviews or additional behavior-paper credits.

study.design: Cross-sectional, voluntary anonymous convenience recruitment through Jordanian academic/professional mailing lists and networks; 525 complete respondents: 353 medical students and 172 ophthalmologists. Recruitment denominator, incomplete-response count and response rate are not supplied. No randomized AI intervention, observed medical decision or actual AI performance comparison.
study.composition: Ophthalmologists: 45 with >10 years practice, 66 with <10 years and 61 residents. Students are 272/353 female versus 80/172 ophthalmologists; age, training and experience differ simultaneously. Cohort contrasts cannot identify causal effects of experience, youth or AI education.
study.demographics: Table 1 reports 35 ophthalmologists over 80 years and 97 aged 48–80. These unusual labels warrant verification against original variables; unusual demographics alone do not prove impossibility, fabrication or a different intended unit. No recoding by conjecture.
study.instrument: The methods call the questionnaire adapted from validated instruments but cite a broad global-eye-health review, reference 3, without naming the original questionnaire or mapping changed items. Alpha .64 and lambda-2 .72 are reported; moderate item-rest correlations are asserted without coefficients. These alone do not establish dimensionality, content validity or measurement equivalence for heterogeneous binary questions. Tau-equivalence is said not to hold without a reported diagnostic.
study.diagnosis: Table 2: 281/353 students and 124/172 ophthalmologists choose human diagnostic expertise, versus 72 and 48 choosing AI. These are stated preferences without matched accuracy, uncertainty, accountability or equivalent task descriptions; they do not establish irrational algorithm aversion.
study.surgery_major_conflict: Table 2 reports 96/172 ophthalmologists favoring AI-assisted surgery, but Table 3 subgroups sum to 9+31+28=68/172, with manual-surgery counts summing to 104 rather than 76. Thus the doctor majority claim differs between tables: 55.8% versus 39.5%. Do not select a preferred table or use this as a reliable pooled adoption estimate.
study.other_cross_table_conflicts: Table 3 versus Table 2 ophthalmologist totals: AI diagnosis 46 vs 48; physician responsibility 117 vs 113; ophthalmology complement 121 vs 120; optometry complement 78 vs 80; skill enhancement 114 vs 110; training collaboration 142 vs 140; AI reliance 10 vs 11; transformative/supportive/disruptive role 53/109/10 vs 54/107/11. Relationship 76/96, expected outcome AI 11 and disparities 43 do agree. This is not one uniform denominator error.
study.within_table_conflicts: Table 3 <10-year training counts 56+11=67 despite N=66. Resident leadership counts 12+22+17=51 despite N=61. Missingness or transcription could explain some problems, but no explanation or respondent-level data selects a correction.
study.conflict_scenarios: When AI advises against surgery and the clinician favors it, prose reports 77% overall, 79% students and 72% doctors; full raw cells for this item are not provided in the main tables. When AI favors surgery and the clinician advises against it, 91% overall favor the clinician, consistent with Table 2 human expected-outcome counts 478/525. Abstract/Results 77–79% omits the doctor figure of 72%.
study.mechanism_boundary: Source identity is confounded with recommending intervention versus nonintervention. Risk aversion, omission preference, decision thresholds, assumed expertise or case framing could contribute. A direction-dependent preference does not uniquely identify trust, omission bias, automation bias or superior caution. Authors explicitly state psychological explanations were not directly measured and remain speculative.
study.responsibility: Table 2 asks physician versus developer responsibility for AI-driven outcomes, 219/353 and 113/172 selecting physicians. The item is not specified as harmful/negligent and offers a binary allocation. It does not measure blame after a defined failure, shared institutional responsibility or legal liability.
study.skills_and_training: Skill reduction is anticipated by 121/353 students and 62/172 doctors, not demonstrated through longitudinal unaided testing. Table 2 training collaboration 277/353=78.5% and 140/172=81.4% differs from the discussion 69–71%. No educational intervention was tested.
study.inference: Authors disclose exploratory hypothesis generation, no multiplicity adjustment and false-positive risk. Reported significance must not be presented as confirmatory, and nonsignificance does not establish equality. Several p-values cannot be reconstructed from the printed counts using the stated chi-square method; raw cells, test definitions and analysis code are needed.

reconstructed_tests.interpretation: No match among these common tests; do not replace the paper value without original data/test details.
Compatible with a Fisher test at reported precision/truncation. The discrepancy with Pearson is not proof of an erroneous result; methods name chi-square only, so clarify test reporting.
Compatible with Pearson. Do not assert all reported tests fail.
Both indicate an exploratory association, but the stated Pearson test does not reconstruct the printed p-value. No causal experience effect follows.
Unresolved test/count disagreement; no significance claim at .05 from either printed value.
Printed cells sum to 162, not 172. Do not silently impute the missing ten or correct the p-value by guesswork.

study.ethics: IRB 25KHCC004 is reported and written informed consent was waived for voluntary survey participation. Do not infer a consent violation from the waiver. The authors declare no generative-AI use; publisher-provided alt-text boilerplate is not contradictory evidence.

summary: No new terms. Enrich existing algorithm-aversion and performance-trust entries with explicitly limited hypothetical-preference evidence; add non-counting boundaries for blame attribution, deskilling and omission bias. Record verifiable denominator/reference corrections and unresolved cross-table/statistical problems without inventing repaired raw data or a new asymmetric-trust mechanism.

findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add a context-specific, explicitly limited survey citation or boundary note rather than another synonym row.

findings.evidence_scope: Hypothetical diagnostic reliability preferences favor human expertise (281/353 students and 124/172 doctors in Table 2). This is context-specific stated acceptance, not a matched-performance behavioral test. Conflicting surgery totals prevent a reliable doctor adoption estimate.
findings.boundary: Human preference can be warranted by task competence, stakes or accountability. No equal-accuracy manipulation, actual delegation, measured harm or universal reluctance is established.

findings.evidence_scope: The survey distinguishes diagnostic reliability, expected surgical outcomes and two opposing advice-conflict scenarios. Ratings and hypothetical choices concern perceived task reliability; surgery totals and the first conflict scenario remain insufficiently reconciled.
findings.boundary: Perceived reliability differs from actual reliability. The source recommending action changes with the intervention direction, so omission/risk preferences cannot be separated from trust. Authors explicitly acknowledge speculative mechanisms.

findings.evidence_scope: A binary physician-versus-developer responsibility item favors physicians in Table 2, but does not specify a negative outcome, fault or negligence. Table 3 totals and the reported group-test p-value disagree with Table 2.
findings.boundary: General responsibility, outcome authorship, prospective duties, blameworthiness and legal liability differ. This boundary note supplies no independent evidence of blame after a defined harmful event or of a legal rule.

findings.evidence_scope: Participants anticipate possible skill reduction; Table 2 lists 121/353 students and 62/172 doctors. No baseline skill, longitudinal change or unaided-performance outcome is measured.
findings.boundary: An expressed concern is not demonstrated loss of acquired competence. Useful assistance, reduced practice, never acquiring a skill and durable skill deterioration require separate evidence; do not count this opinion survey as proof of deskilling.

source_corrections.correction: With the student denominator 353, 166/353=47.0%. The printed 74% equals 166/225 of all AI-experienced respondents, a different denominator from the other cohort percentages. Preserve 166 as the reported count and disclose the denominator inconsistency.
source_corrections.scope: Direct arithmetic and visual table check; not a raw-data correction.

source_corrections.correction: The displayed counts imply 34.3% and 68.0%, respectively. Confirm original data before choosing whether counts or labels were intended.
source_corrections.scope: Within-table arithmetic; cross-table conflicts remain unresolved.

source_corrections.correction: Table 2 reports 277/353 and 140/172, approximately 78–81% (417/525 overall). Table 3 also conflicts with doctor training counts. Attribute the figures to their specific locations rather than silently select one as ground truth.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The surgery preference total differs by 28 doctors, reversing whether a doctor majority supports AI surgery. Several other totals disagree, and two subgroup columns do not equal their stated sample sizes. Original data and table-generation code are necessary; no corrected values are asserted.

Abstract/Results 77–79% does not include the doctors’ 72% figure later reported. The first scenario’s full raw table is unavailable in the main PDF. No reconstructed contingency test or causal explanation is credited.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: PDF page 2, instrument attribution and page 7 reference 3
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The only cited source for adapted validated instruments is Tan et al., Artificial intelligence and digital health in global eye health: opportunities and challenges, Lancet Global Health 11(9), e1432–e1443 (2023), DOI 10.1016/S2214-109X(23)00323-6. Metadata identifies a broad review, not the original questionnaire. Obtain the original item source and validation mapping; do not claim the instrument has never been validated.

Selected reconstruction details are retained in study.reconstructed_tests. Fisher can explain the Table 2 surgery p-value, but several other values remain unresolved. Do not conflate unreported test choice, count disagreement and confirmed computational error.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: PDF pages 4–6, causal and legal interpretations
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Experience-group differences do not test the effect of training or digital familiarity. Survey allocations cannot establish that ultimate legal responsibility always belongs to clinicians. Specific surgery/trust/education claims require direct matching sources rather than broad diagnosis/fairness/black-box references alone.

methodological_limits: Convenience regional sample, unknown response denominator and incomplete-case losses; cohort composition and experience/age/training confounded.
Hypothetical forced choices without matched accuracy or full supplied wording; source and intervention direction confounded in disagreement scenarios.
Unresolved reporting conflicts substantially limit numerical synthesis; do not use this paper as reliable evidence of a doctor majority favoring AI surgery.
Reliability coefficients do not establish a unitary construct, validity, item equivalence or demonstrated deskilling; no measured psychological mediator.
Exploratory unadjusted multiple tests, no equivalence inference from null results and no causal training or clinical-safety inference.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Both papers assess healthcare opinions, but Rolison concerns fictional physiotherapy prioritization among UK public respondents, whereas this paper concerns students/doctors and ophthalmology. Do not pool different populations, tasks or subjective measures as one clinical AI trust effect.

As with mismatched plotted and tabulated condemnation means in Keijsers, preserve conflicting surgery totals explicitly; matching direction in some comparisons does not authorize silently repairing the source.

Check actual test variants before declaring p-values wrong: Fisher can account for Table 2 surgery just as a one-sided test can account for the earlier t-test threshold. Other unresolved values still require original data.

deferred.reason: Descriptive label for existing context-sensitive reliability preferences, with nonintervention and source cues confounded; no uniquely identified new mechanism.

deferred.reason: Cross-sectional association with unresolved tables; education and experience effects were not randomized or directly tested.

deferred.term: Human handover / bias mitigation / therapeutic relationship decline
deferred.reason: Stated preferences and concerns do not demonstrate actual handover, discriminatory output reduction or longitudinal relationship effects.

limitations: No new entries, synthetic timeline series, independent credits for unread references, raw-data repair, automatic ethical/harm edges or clinical recommendations.
